title: Zeta Value Definition
content: Defines $\zeta(s)$ as a tsum over natural numbers: `zetaValue s = ∑' n, 1 / n^s`. This is a clean Lean representation where the $n=0$ term vanishes (since $0^s = 0$ for $s > 0$, making $1/0^s$ undefined but handled by Lean's division-by-zero convention). The definition is `noncomputable` because real number arithmetic in Lean is noncomputable by default.
mathContext: $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s} = \texttt{tsum}\left(n \mapsto \frac{1}{n^s}\right)$ where the $n=0$ term is $0$ by convention.

title: Basel Problem: ζ(2) = π²/6
content: Derives $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ directly from Mathlib's `hasSum_zeta_two`. The proof pattern is elegant: unfold the tsum definition, then extract the equality from the HasSum witness using `.tsum_eq`. This is the celebrated Basel problem, first solved by Euler in 1734 using a daring manipulation of infinite products that he later justified rigorously.
relatedConcepts: Euler's formula for even zeta values

title: ζ(4) = π⁴/90
content: Derives $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$ from Mathlib's `hasSum_zeta_four`, following the same pattern as $\zeta(2)$. These are the only two even zeta values currently in Mathlib — higher values $\zeta(6), \zeta(8), \ldots$ follow the same Bernoulli number formula but aren't yet formalized.

title: Lindemann's Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes Lindemann's 1882 theorem: $\pi$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$. This is a consequence of the deeper Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem (if $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are algebraic and linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, then $e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are algebraically independent). Applied with $\alpha = i\pi$ and $e^{i\pi} = -1$, this gives transcendence of $\pi$. Not yet in Mathlib v4.26.0, so it must be axiomatized.
mathContext: $\pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, i.e., $\pi$ is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients.

title: Apery's Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes Roger Apery's celebrated 1978 result: $\zeta(3)$ is irrational. Apery stunned the mathematical community by constructing two rapidly converging sequences of rationals whose limit is $\zeta(3)$, with convergence fast enough to establish irrationality via a criterion of Nesterenko. The proof was initially met with skepticism at the Journees Arithmetiques in Marseille, until van der Poorten and Cohen verified the details.

title: Transcendence Conjecture for Odd Zeta Values
content: Defines the transcendence conjecture as a Lean `Prop`: all $\zeta(2k+1)$ for $k \geq 1$ are transcendental. This is far beyond current techniques — we cannot even prove transcendence of $\zeta(3)$, the most accessible case. The conjecture is parametrized by $k \geq 1$, covering $\zeta(3), \zeta(5), \zeta(7), \ldots$

title: Irrationality Conjecture for Odd Zeta Values
content: Defines the weaker irrationality conjecture: all $\zeta(2k+1)$ are irrational. While we know infinitely many are irrational (Rivoal 2000), we cannot prove irrationality for any specific $\zeta(2k+1)$ beyond $\zeta(3)$. The gap between this conjecture and the transcendence conjecture is enormous.

title: Transcendence Implies Irrationality
content: Sorry-free proof that the transcendence conjecture implies the irrationality conjecture, using Mathlib's `Transcendental.irrational`. This is the top link in the implication chain: every transcendental number is irrational (by contrapositive, since rationals are algebraic).
mathContext: If $\alpha$ is transcendental then $\alpha$ is irrational (contrapositive: $\mathbb{Q} \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$).

title: Conjecture Specializes to Apery
content: Specializes the irrationality conjecture at $k=1$ to recover Apery's theorem: $\zeta(2 \cdot 1 + 1) = \zeta(3)$ is irrational. Uses `le_rfl` to discharge the $1 \leq 1$ side condition. A pure structural argument with no mathematical content beyond universal instantiation.

title: Conjecture Gives Both ζ(3) and ζ(5) Irrational
content: Further demonstrates the conjecture's strength by extracting both $\zeta(3)$ and $\zeta(5)$ irrationality as a conjunction. Uses `omega` to discharge the $1 \leq 2$ condition for $k=2$.

title: The Even/Odd Divide
content: Defines `even_zeta_rational_multiple`: $\zeta(2k) = q \cdot \pi^{2k}$ for some nonzero rational $q$. This captures Euler's discovery that even zeta values are rational multiples of powers of $\pi$. The contrast with odd values is profound: no odd zeta value has any known closed form involving $\pi$ or other standard constants. Zagier called this divide 'one of the most tantalizing mysteries in number theory.'

title: ζ(2) Transcendence (Sorry Target)
content: Asserts $\zeta(2)$ is transcendental with sorry on the algebraic manipulation. The proof strategy: $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$, so if $\zeta(2)$ were algebraic, then $\pi^2 = 6\zeta(2)$ would be algebraic (algebraic numbers form a field), hence $\pi$ would be algebraic — contradicting Lindemann. The sorry is on the Mathlib gap: closure of algebraic numbers under field operations and $n$th roots.
mathContext: $\pi^2/6$ algebraic $\Rightarrow$ $\pi^2$ algebraic $\Rightarrow$ $\pi$ algebraic $\Rightarrow$ contradiction with Lindemann.

title: ζ(4) Transcendence (Sorry Target)
content: Same argument as $\zeta(2)$ transcendence, now for $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$. Both sorry targets await Mathlib's algebraic closure API — specifically that rational multiples of transcendental powers remain transcendental. These are prime candidates for Aristotle automated proof search.

title: Rivoal's Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes Tanguy Rivoal's breakthrough 2000 result: the set of $k$ such that $\zeta(2k+1)$ is irrational is infinite. Rivoal's proof uses very-well-poised hypergeometric series to construct explicit linear forms in odd zeta values. The precise quantitative result is stronger: $\dim_\mathbb{Q} \langle 1, \zeta(3), \zeta(5), \ldots, \zeta(s) \rangle \geq \frac{1+o(1)}{1+\log 2} \log s$. The formalization uses `Set.Infinite` for cleaner compositionality.

title: Zudilin's Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes Wadim Zudilin's 2001 refinement: at least one of $\zeta(5), \zeta(7), \zeta(9), \zeta(11)$ is irrational. Formalized as a 4-way `Or` disjunction. Zudilin narrowed Rivoal's infinite existential to a finite explicit set by optimizing hypergeometric parameters. The gap between this and proving irrationality of any single $\zeta(2k+1)$ for $k \geq 2$ remains one of the most frustrating barriers in the field.

title: Conjecture Implies Rivoal
content: Sorry-free proof that the irrationality conjecture subsumes Rivoal's theorem. Uses `Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem` with the injection $n \mapsto n+1$: if every $\zeta(2(n+1)+1)$ is irrational, the set of witnesses is infinite. This is a clean structural argument using Mathlib's set-theoretic infrastructure rather than manual cardinality reasoning.
mathContext: If $f: \mathbb{N} \to S$ is injective and $\text{ran}(f) \subseteq S$, then $S$ is infinite. Here $f(n) = n+1$.

title: Conjecture Implies Zudilin
content: Shows the irrationality conjecture implies Zudilin's theorem by providing the first disjunct: $\zeta(5)$ is irrational (specializing at $k=2$). Uses `Or.inl` to inhabit the 4-way disjunction. The simplest theorem in the file, but structurally important for the implication hierarchy.

title: The Grand Unification Theorem
content: The culminating result `conjecture_implies_all_known`: the transcendence conjecture alone recovers Apery's theorem, Rivoal's theorem, and Zudilin's theorem as corollaries. Derived sorry-free by first passing through the irrationality conjecture and then applying the three specialization theorems. This demonstrates the transcendence conjecture as a single organizing principle subsuming all partial results accumulated over 1978-2001.

title: Problem Status: OPEN
content: A simple string recording the problem status. No odd zeta value is known to be transcendental as of 2026. Even the most accessible case, $\zeta(3)$ transcendence, appears to require fundamentally new techniques beyond current methods.
